title: Docker logs crashes every couple of hours
body: Every couple of hours, `docker compose logs` crashes on my production servers. The daemon first reports an error such as `error unmarshalling log entry (size=108554): proto: LogEntry: illegal tag 0 (wire type 6)`, followed by repeated errors such as `log message is too large (1937007727 > 1000000)`. A manually bounded `docker logs --since ... --until ...` request can trigger the same error. This affects two AWS EC2 production environments running nginx-based workloads. They use the `awslogs` driver to send logs to CloudWatch. CloudWatch appears to receive all entries, but the locally cached logs can lose several hours after the error. I could not find a genuinely huge or unusual application log entry, reproduce the problem reliably, or import the cached files into a dummy container. The affected Docker Engine version is 20.10.23.

symptoms_visible: `docker compose logs` crashes every couple of hours on one production environment and roughly weekly on another.
The daemon reports an illegal protobuf tag while unmarshalling a cached log entry, then reports implausible message sizes as large as nearly 2 GB.
CloudWatch still contains the application logs, while `docker logs` can stop early and omit several hours from the local view.
N0.label: N0 recurring local log-read failure reported

symptoms_visible: After I temporarily switched the most problematic instance to the local driver, `docker compose logs` was still running and the instance was healthy about twenty hours later.
During that probe, the container logs were available through `docker logs`, but my access and error logs were not reaching their usual CloudWatch destination.
N1.label: N1 local-driver configuration probe

symptoms_visible: A fresh export of an affected container's cached logs looks unusual, and `less` treats it as a binary file.
N2.label: N2 affected cached log supplied

symptoms_visible: All of my AWS environments are currently reporting healthy even though we did not change our application stacks or logging mechanism.
The servers receive automatic updates and are now on the Amazon Linux platform release identified as 3.7.1.
N3.label: N3 failures no longer observed after automatic platform update

symptoms_visible: My environments remain healthy, but the previously exported cached file still contains the data associated with the unmarshalling and oversized-message failures.
N4.label: N4 cached-log corruption diagnosed

symptoms_visible: I have not retested an affected environment on a Docker build containing the new corrupt-log recovery behavior.
N_terminal.label: terminal fix released without reporter retest

question_patterns: Can you temporarily use the local logging driver on the most frequently affected instance and report whether the log-reading error returns?
Could you test a different logging driver on one affected environment and tell us how long it remains healthy?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I switched the most problematic instance from `awslog` to `local`. After about twenty hours, `docker compose logs` was still running and the instance was healthy. I could read all the container logs manually with `docker logs`, although my access and error logs were no longer reaching CloudWatch.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The same unmarshalling and oversized-message errors returned within a few minutes while using newly created local-driver logs.
The instance stayed healthy for eighteen hours instead of twenty, with the same CloudWatch limitation.

edges.comment: Reporter messages c13-c14 only. This was a handler-directed production configuration probe of the reporter's most problematic AWS instance. Per the measurement-class rule, its outcome is evidence rather than the final fix; it does not establish that awslogs encoding caused the corruption.

question_patterns: Can you inspect and provide one of the affected container log files from `/var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/local-logs`?
Could you share a cached log file from a period when the error occurred, if its contents can be provided safely?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I downloaded a fresh export from an environment that had the issue. The logs look weird and `less` considers the file binary. I sent the affected Docker container logs privately because they may contain sensitive data.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The file is ordinary readable text with valid records throughout, and a byte-for-byte integrity check shows no damaged or zero-filled region.
Another viewer also classifies the same file as binary, and I provide it through a different private channel.

edges.comment: Reporter messages c21, c27, in response to participant5 c20/c24. The private file itself is unavailable as a benchmark attachment, so only the reporter's actual observation and transfer are represented.

question_patterns: Are the affected environments still failing, and did anything change on them?
Did you change the application or logging setup before the environments started reporting healthy?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: All of my AWS environments are reporting healthy now. We did not update our technology stacks or change the logging mechanism. The servers do receive automatic updates, and the environments are all on `Docker running on 64bit Amazon Linux 2/3.7.1` now.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The errors are still occurring daily on the unchanged platform, including in newly created log files.
The environment names were changed, but the platform and logging configuration stayed identical.

question_patterns: Did your team deploy any application or logging configuration change that could explain the recovery?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: No. Nothing changed on our side as far as I am aware; we did not change the application stacks or logging mechanism.

edges.comment: Reporter messages c25, c27, c29, answering participant4 c28. These facts describe the reporter's AWS fleet only. The separate Ubuntu/IBM local-driver case from participant2 is deliberately not merged into this causal chain.

solution.intent: Diagnose the implausible message length as a damaged framed local log file: once the reader loses record alignment, it interprets bytes from the middle of damaged data as the next message length and cannot recover within that file.
solution.concrete_example: The local format stores a message length, the protobuf message, and another length. If the file is corrupted, the reader can start in the middle of data and interpret arbitrary bytes as a huge length. On older versions, remove the damaged log file; a `--since`, `--until`, or `--tail` request may avoid it if the request excludes the corrupted file.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the error sequence and an affected file that appeared binary. Mapping those observations to the local driver's length/message/length framing and concluding that a length was read from the middle of corrupt data was participant5's engineering analysis in c30.

edges.comment: Participant5 c30, applied to the reporter's original cached-log failure. This is the first corruption diagnosis, not yet the later resilient-reader fix. The maintainer could not reproduce corruption under concurrent reads, writes, and aggressive rotation.

solution.intent: Use a Docker/Moby build containing the resilient local-log reader, which treats a decoding failure as corruption, skips the remainder of that damaged log file, and continues with the next file instead of terminating the entire logs request.
solution.concrete_example: Upgrade to Moby v27.4.0 or newer, or v28, where the reader recovery was backported or included. The maintainer's final explanation is that sudden shutdowns can leave zero-filled data in an in-progress preallocated log write, especially with ext4's default metadata-only journaling. The updated reader records the decoding condition, skips the rest of that file, and proceeds to the next rotated file.
solution.inference_hint: The final accepted diagnosis in c31 supersedes the earlier awslogs/local-driver encoding theory: corrupt on-disk local log records are most likely produced by incomplete writes during power loss or another sudden shutdown. The resilient-reader behavior and release status were reported by the maintainer; the original reporter did not return to test such a build.

edges.comment: Final maintainer resolution in c31. The recovery shipped in Moby v28 and was backported to v27.4.0 and later. No affected reporter confirmed the released fix on their own system, so the terminal records availability of the fix but user_perceives_resolved remains false.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause as corruption of the framed local cache log, causing the reader to lose record alignment and interpret damaged bytes as an implausibly large message length.

Must explain that sudden shutdowns or power failures are the likely source of corruption because an in-progress filesystem write can leave zero-filled or incomplete data; this diagnosis must be grounded in the unmarshalling error, huge length values, missing local records, and binary-looking cached file.

Must recommend updating to a build containing the resilient log reader that skips the remainder of a corrupt file and continues with the next log file; deleting or excluding the corrupt file is only a legacy recovery option.
Must not present the earlier awslogs-versus-local encoding mismatch or the Amazon logger-rate-limit patch as the final root cause.
Must not treat the temporary healthy local-driver probe as proof that changing logging drivers permanently fixes the underlying corruption.
Must ask the reporter to verify on a build containing the reader recovery fix before declaring the issue resolved, because the reporter never confirmed that released fix.

persona_hint.experience_level: Production operator with moderate Docker and AWS experience. Comfortable using SSH, inspecting daemon logs, changing a logging driver for a controlled test, downloading container cache files, and running package-inspection commands, but explicitly defers low-level protobuf and Docker internals analysis to maintainers.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, cooperative, and cautious. Reports elapsed test results and exact errors, distinguishes observations from guesses, raises operational concerns about production changes, and follows up when progress stalls.
